Akku tried to create a small business empire; he extorted money, harming and threatening those who resisted him. During his life as a criminal, Akku murdered at least three individuals. He tortured and kidnapped people, invaded homes, and raped over 40 women and girls. He bribed police, giving them money and buying them drinks to convince them to let him continue committing crimes. As a result, the police not only refused to stop Akku for many years, but supported him. Akku and his associates gang-raped women and girls as young as age 10 as a "warning" to those who resisted him. There's a documentary about this.

item.title: GovBrief Today #610
item.description: Reporters started a private school in Arkansas with $45 and an American flag. They aren't teachers and don't intend to run a school. ProPublica and three local newsrooms wanted to see how easily states approve new private schools and send them tax money. They tried in three states and succeeded in two. In West Virginia, they filed their paperwork by hand on notebook paper. Nobody asked about their qualifications or what they planned to teach. Arkansas law requires schools to display an American flag, so they bought a small one at a Little Rock shop to sit on a newsroom cubicle. Then a state education employee called back with advice on how their school could start collecting $7,208 a student in tax money. They could enroll students tomorrow. I've emailed 9,356 stories over 610 straight nights, free and without ads. The algorithm can't show them all to you. Add your email address at govbrief.today and I will.
